The statement depicts an adverse supply-shock environment (pandemic aftereffects, energy prices, Ukraine war, China lockdowns) keeping inflation elevated while weighing on output, with the Fed tightening via a 50 bp hike to 0.75–1% and the start of balance-sheet reduction. SLOOS (April 2022) indicates bank credit was still broadly supportive at that time: domestic banks eased standards for C&I loans to large and middle-market firms and for multifamily CRE, left other CRE standards largely unchanged, and saw stronger loan demand for inventories, receivables, equipment, and plant investment, alongside lower costs on credit lines. Consumer credit conditions also eased (e.g., credit cards), with stronger demand for HELOCs and auto loans, though banks reported weaker demand for residential real estate loans; foreign banks tightened C&I standards. These SLOOS findings temper the downside tone from financial stability risks by suggesting credit availability and loan demand were still supporting activity in early Q2, even as interest-sensitive sectors were starting to cool. Adjusted net tone: cautiously negative, but less so than without SLOOS.
